report:
## Conclusion

**No.** High-quality evidence indicates that saw palmetto (*Serenoa repens*) preparations do **not** meaningfully improve urinary symptoms from benign prostatic hyperplasia compared with placebo in the longer term.

The updated Cochrane review found **little to no difference** in symptom scores at **12–17 months**: mean difference in International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) **0.07 points** (95% CI −0.75 to 0.88; 3 studies, 898 participants; high-certainty evidence). This is far below a clinically noticeable improvement. [https://www.cochrane.org/zh-hans/evidence/CD001423_serenoa-repens-benign-prostatic-hyperplasia](https://www.cochrane.org/zh-hans/evidence/CD001423_serenoa-repens-benign-prostatic-hyperplasia)

This conclusion is consistent with a large randomized trial in which men received progressively higher saw-palmetto doses or placebo over 72 weeks; the trial found no improvement in lower urinary-tract symptoms, urinary-flow measures, or prostate size with saw palmetto. [https://archive.connect.h1.co/article/717969419/](https://archive.connect.h1.co/article/717969419/)

A recent evidence summary for clinicians likewise concludes that saw palmetto does not reduce BPH-associated symptoms versus placebo, while serious adverse effects were not significantly increased. [https://www.aafp.org/afp/2024/0500/cochrane-saw-palmetto-benign-prostatic-hyperplasia](https://www.aafp.org/afp/2024/0500/cochrane-saw-palmetto-benign-prostatic-hyperplasia)

Thus, saw palmetto is generally not supported as an effective long-term treatment for BPH symptoms. Persistent, worsening, or bothersome urinary symptoms merit clinician assessment, since they can require evidence-based medication or evaluation for other causes.
